questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following is a fundamental (base) physical quantity?
questions.explanation: Mass, length, time, electric current, temperature, luminous intensity and amount of substance are the seven fundamental (base) quantities; force, velocity and pressure are all derived from these.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following is a derived physical quantity?
questions.explanation: Force is derived from the base quantities mass, length and time (F = ma, with dimensions MLT-2), unlike time, length and mass, which are themselves base quantities.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The S.I. base unit of mass is the
questions.explanation: The kilogram (kg) is the S.I. base unit of mass; the newton is a derived unit of force, while the gram and pound are non-S.I. or subunit measures.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimension of velocity is
questions.explanation: Velocity = distance/time, so its dimension is L (length) divided by T (time), giving LT-1.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimension of force (F = ma) is
questions.explanation: Force = mass x acceleration. Acceleration has dimension LT-2, so force has dimension M x LT-2 = MLT-2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimension of pressure (force per unit area) is
questions.explanation: Pressure = force/area = MLT-2 / L2 = ML-1T-2, since area has dimension L2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Dimensional analysis is mainly used to
options: calculate the efficiency of a machine
check the homogeneity (consistency) of a physical equation
determine the direction of a vector quantity
measure the exact numerical value of a physical quantity
questions.explanation: Dimensional analysis verifies that the dimensions on both sides of an equation match, confirming the equation is dimensionally consistent, though it cannot supply dimensionless numerical constants.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which pair of physical quantities has the same dimensions?
questions.explanation: Work and energy are both measured in joules and share the dimension ML2T-2, since energy is simply the capacity to do work; the other pairs have different dimensions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Rectilinear motion refers to the motion of a body
options: that has zero velocity at all times
questions.explanation: Rectilinear motion is motion confined to a straight line, as opposed to circular or curved (projectile) motion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In the equation of motion v = u + at, the symbol 'a' represents the
questions.explanation: In v = u + at, u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, t is time, and a is the constant (uniform) acceleration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body starts with a velocity of 4 m/s and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s2 for 6 s. What is its final velocity?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body with initial velocity 5 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s2 for 4 s. Using s = ut + 1/2 at^2, what distance does it cover?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is dropped from rest and falls a vertical distance of 20 m. Using v^2 = u^2 + 2as and g = 10 m/s2, what is its velocity just before hitting the ground?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A stone dropped from rest takes 4 s to hit the ground. Using s = 1/2 gt^2 and g = 10 m/s2, from what height was it dropped?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s2, how long does it take to reach its maximum height?
questions.explanation: At maximum height, final vertical velocity is zero, so t = u/g = 20/10 = 2 s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s2, what maximum height does it reach?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A projectile is launched with a velocity of 20 m/s at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Using g = 10 m/s2, what is its time of flight? (sin 30 degrees = 0.5)
questions.explanation: Time of flight T = 2u sin(theta)/g = 2(20)(0.5)/10 = 20/10 = 2 s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For the same projectile (u = 20 m/s, angle = 30 degrees, g = 10 m/s2), what is the maximum height reached? (sin 30 degrees = 0.5)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For the same projectile (u = 20 m/s, angle = 30 degrees, g = 10 m/s2), what is its horizontal range R = u^2 sin(2 theta)/g? (sin 60 degrees is approximately 0.87)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: During projectile motion (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal component of the velocity
questions.explanation: Since gravity acts only vertically, there is no horizontal acceleration, so the horizontal velocity component stays constant throughout the projectile's flight.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Inertia is best described as the property of a body that makes it
options: resist any change in its state of rest or uniform motion
always move in a circular path
questions.explanation: Inertia is the natural tendency of matter to remain in its existing state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force, and is the basis of Newton's First Law.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Newton's First Law of Motion states that a body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless
options: it is released from a height
an external unbalanced force acts on it
it is placed in a vacuum
questions.explanation: This is the law of inertia: a net external force is required to change a body's velocity (speed or direction).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Newton's Second Law of Motion is expressed mathematically as
questions.explanation: Newton's Second Law states that the net force on a body equals the rate of change of momentum, which for constant mass reduces to F = ma.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A resultant force of 20 N is applied to a mass of 5 kg. What acceleration is produced?
questions.explanation: Using F = ma: a = F/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Newton's Third Law of Motion states that
options: a body at rest has no inertia
force is directly proportional to acceleration
for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law describes the mutual, paired nature of forces: any force exerted by one body on a second is matched by an equal and opposite force from the second on the first.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Linear momentum of a body is defined as the product of its
questions.explanation: Momentum p = mv, a vector quantity pointing in the same direction as the body's velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body of mass 3 kg moves with a velocity of 4 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass x velocity = 3 x 4 = 12 kg m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Impulse delivered to a body is defined as the
options: product of the force applied and the time for which it acts, equal to the change in momentum
product of force and distance moved
product of mass and velocity only
questions.explanation: Impulse = F x t = change in momentum (mv - mu), linking the force-time effect of an impact to the resulting momentum change.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum states that in the absence of external forces, the total momentum of a system of colliding bodies
options: remains constant before and after collision
questions.explanation: Provided no external (unbalanced) force acts on the system, total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after, whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 4 kg trolley and they stick together. What is their common velocity after collision?
questions.explanation: By conservation of momentum: total momentum before = 2(6) + 4(0) = 12 kg m/s. Combined mass = 6 kg, so common velocity = 12/6 = 2 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A collision in which both kinetic energy and momentum are conserved is called
questions.explanation: In a perfectly elastic collision, the bodies bounce apart such that both total momentum and total kinetic energy are unchanged; in inelastic collisions, kinetic energy is not conserved (some is lost as heat/sound/deformation).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The coefficient of static friction between two surfaces is the ratio of the
options: limiting frictional force to the normal reaction between the surfaces
normal reaction to the limiting frictional force
applied force to the weight of the object
weight of the object to the area of contact
questions.explanation: Coefficient of friction (mu) = limiting friction (F) / normal reaction (R). If the normal reaction is 50 N and the limiting friction is 20 N, mu = 20/50 = 0.4.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The centripetal force acting on a body moving in a circular path is given by the formula
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is the net force directed towards the centre of the circular path, required to keep the body moving in that path, given by F = mv^2/r.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 2 kg object moves in a circle of radius 5 m at a speed of 10 m/s. What centripetal force acts on it?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with a linear speed of 2 m/s. What is its angular velocity (omega = v/r)?
questions.explanation: Angular velocity omega = v/r = 2/0.5 = 4 rad/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Roads are banked at bends mainly to
options: provide part of the centripetal force needed, reducing reliance on friction alone
increase the frictional force between tyres and road
reduce the speed of vehicles automatically
questions.explanation: Banking tilts the road so that a component of the normal reaction contributes to the centripetal force, allowing vehicles to safely negotiate bends at higher speeds with less dependence on friction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The period of a simple pendulum is given by the formula
questions.explanation: For small oscillations, the period of a simple pendulum depends only on its length (l) and the acceleration due to gravity (g), given by T = 2(pi) sqrt(l/g).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A simple pendulum has a length of 1 m. Using g = 10 m/s2, what is its period? (pi is approximately 3.14)
questions.explanation: T = 2(pi) sqrt(l/g) = 2(3.14) sqrt(1/10) = 6.28 x 0.316 = approximately 1.99 s, i.e. about 2.0 s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The period of oscillation of a mass on a spring is given by the formula
questions.explanation: For a mass m attached to a spring of force constant k undergoing SHM, the period is T = 2(pi) sqrt(m/k).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A mass of 0.5 kg is attached to a spring of force constant 50 N/m. What is the period of oscillation? (pi is approximately 3.14)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Simple Harmonic Motion, the frequency (f) is related to the period (T) by
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second, the reciprocal of the period: f = 1/T.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Simple Harmonic Motion, at the extreme positions of oscillation, the body's velocity and acceleration are respectively
questions.explanation: At the extreme (turning) points, the body is momentarily at rest (velocity = 0), while the restoring force, and hence acceleration, is at its greatest magnitude, directed back towards equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act at right angles to each other on a body. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.explanation: For perpendicular forces, resultant = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The equilibrant of a system of forces is a single force that is
options: always twice the magnitude of the resultant
equal in magnitude and direction to the resultant
equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the resultant
questions.explanation: The equilibrant exactly balances the resultant of a set of forces, being equal in size but acting in the opposite direction, so that the body remains in equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The moment of a force about a point is defined as the product of the
options: distance and time taken to apply the force
force and the mass of the object
force and the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force
questions.explanation: Moment (torque) = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, measuring the turning effect of the force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A force of 10 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 0.5 m from a pivot. What moment does it produce?
questions.explanation: Moment = force x perpendicular distance = 10 x 0.5 = 5 Nm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A couple consists of
options: two equal, opposite, parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide, producing rotation only
a single force acting at the centre of gravity
two equal forces acting along the same line, producing no rotation
two unequal forces acting in the same direction
questions.explanation: A couple has zero resultant force (since the forces are equal and opposite) but produces a net turning moment because the forces act along different, parallel lines.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A uniform rod is pivoted at its centre. A weight of 5 N hangs at 20 cm from the pivot on one side. What weight must hang at 30 cm from the pivot on the other side to balance the rod?
questions.explanation: By the Principle of Moments: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. 5 x 20 = W x 30, so W = 100/30 = 3.33 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Principle of Moments states that when a body is in rotational equilibrium, the
options: resultant of all forces must act through the centre of gravity only
sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point
net force acting on the body must be greater than zero
body must be moving at constant velocity
questions.explanation: This is the condition for rotational (moment) equilibrium: the turning effects in each direction about any chosen pivot must balance exactly.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A rigid body is in complete equilibrium under coplanar forces when
options: only the resultant force is zero
all the forces are equal in magnitude
the resultant force is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero
only the resultant moment is zero
questions.explanation: Complete equilibrium requires both translational equilibrium (zero net force, so no acceleration) and rotational equilibrium (zero net moment, so no angular acceleration).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The centre of gravity of a body is the point through which
options: the body's total mass becomes concentrated to zero
the body always rotates when spun
the entire weight of the body may be considered to act
questions.explanation: The centre of gravity is the single point at which the resultant of the weights of all the particles making up the body can be considered to act.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body is in neutral equilibrium if, when slightly displaced, it
options: moves further away and topples over
stays in its new position without moving further or returning
questions.explanation: In neutral equilibrium (e.g. a ball resting on a flat horizontal surface), the height of the centre of gravity does not change on displacement, so the body simply remains in its new position.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Work done by a force is given by the formula
questions.explanation: Work done W = Fs cos(theta), where F is the force, s is the displacement, and theta is the angle between the force and the direction of displacement.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A force of 20 N moves an object 5 m in a direction making 60 degrees with the force. How much work is done? (cos 60 degrees = 0.5)
questions.explanation: W = Fs cos(theta) = 20 x 5 x cos(60 degrees) = 100 x 0.5 = 50 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body of mass 4 kg moves with a velocity of 5 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body of mass 2 kg is raised to a height of 10 m. Using g = 10 m/s2, what is its gravitational potential energy?
questions.explanation: PE = mgh = 2 x 10 x 10 = 200 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy states that in the absence of friction and other resistive forces,
options: total energy always increases as a body falls
potential energy is always converted entirely to heat
the sum of kinetic and potential energy of a system remains constant
kinetic energy is always equal to potential energy
questions.explanation: Where only gravity does work (no friction or air resistance), the total mechanical energy (KE + PE) of a system remains constant, though it may change form as the body moves.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object falls freely from rest through a height of 20 m. Using g = 10 m/s2 and energy conservation, what is its velocity just before hitting the ground?
questions.explanation: Loss in PE = gain in KE: mgh = 1/2 mv^2, so v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 20) = sqrt(400) = 20 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A machine does 600 J of work in 20 seconds. What is its power output?
questions.explanation: Power = Work/time = 600/20 = 30 W.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A pulley system is used to lift a load of 150 N with an effort of 30 N. What is its mechanical advantage?
questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage (MA) = load/effort = 150/30 = 5.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An inclined plane 10 m long is used to raise a load to a height of 2 m. What is its velocity ratio?
questions.explanation: Velocity ratio (VR) = distance moved by effort/distance moved by load = length of incline/height = 10/2 = 5.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A machine has a mechanical advantage of 4 and a velocity ratio of 5. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100% = (4/5) x 100% = 80%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a hydraulic press, the small piston has an area of 5 cm^2 and the large piston has an area of 50 cm^2. If an effort is applied on the small piston to lift a load on the large piston, what is the velocity ratio (ratio of areas)?
questions.explanation: Since pressure is transmitted equally (Pascal's principle), the force (and velocity) ratio equals the ratio of the piston areas: VR = A(large)/A(small) = 50/5 = 10.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A gear system has a driver gear with 20 teeth engaged with a driven gear with 60 teeth. What is the velocity ratio of the system?
questions.explanation: Velocity ratio of gears = number of teeth on driven gear/number of teeth on driver gear = 60/20 = 3.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Hooke's Law states that within the elastic limit, the extension produced in a spring is
options: proportional to the square of the applied force
inversely proportional to the applied force
directly proportional to the applied force
questions.explanation: Hooke's Law: F = ke, so the extension (or compression) e is directly proportional to the applied force F, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A spring extends by 4 cm when a load of 20 N is applied. What is its spring constant?
questions.explanation: Spring constant k = F/e = 20 N / 4 cm = 5 N/cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Tensile stress in a material under a stretching force is defined as the
options: force applied per unit cross-sectional area
extension produced per unit cross-sectional area
extension produced per unit original length
questions.explanation: Tensile stress = F/A, the applied force divided by the cross-sectional area over which it acts, measured in pascals (N/m^2).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Tensile strain in a stretched wire is defined as the
options: extension produced per unit original length
force applied per unit cross-sectional area
questions.explanation: Tensile strain = extension/original length (e/L), a dimensionless ratio describing the fractional deformation of the material.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wire of original length 1 m and cross-sectional area 2 x 10^-6 m^2 stretches by 0.5 x 10^-3 m under a force of 100 N. What is its Young's modulus?
questions.explanation: Stress = F/A = 100/(2 x 10^-6) = 5 x 10^7 Pa. Strain = e/L = (0.5 x 10^-3)/1 = 5 x 10^-4. Young's modulus = stress/strain = (5 x 10^7)/(5 x 10^-4) = 1 x 10^11 Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The energy stored in a spring stretched by an extension x under a force F (within the elastic limit) is given by
questions.explanation: The elastic potential energy stored equals the area under the force-extension graph, a triangle, giving energy = 1/2 Fx (equivalently 1/2 kx^2).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A spring stretches by 4 cm (0.04 m) under a force of 20 N. How much elastic potential energy is stored in it?
questions.explanation: Energy stored = 1/2 Fx = 0.5 x 20 x 0.04 = 0.4 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The elastic limit of a material is the point beyond which the material
options: cannot be stretched any further under any force
no longer returns to its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed
questions.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit, a material undergoes permanent (plastic) deformation and does not fully recover its original dimensions once the force is removed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Density of a substance is defined as its
questions.explanation: Density (rho) = mass/volume, typically measured in kg/m^3 or g/cm^3.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body has a mass of 500 g and a volume of 200 cm^3. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Convert to S.I. units: mass = 0.5 kg, volume = 200 cm^3 = 2 x 10^-4 m^3. Density = 0.5/(2 x 10^-4) = 2500 kg/m3.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The relative density of a substance is defined as the ratio of the
options: density of the substance to the density of water
density of water to the density of the substance
mass of the substance to its volume
weight of the substance to its mass
questions.explanation: Relative density (specific gravity) = density of substance / density of water, a dimensionless number since both densities are in the same units.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object weighs 50 N in air and 30 N when fully submerged in water. What is its relative density, using the apparent loss of weight method?
questions.explanation: Relative density = weight in air / (weight in air - weight in water) = 50/(50-30) = 50/20 = 2.5.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The pressure exerted at a depth h in a liquid of density (rho) is given by
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure at depth h is P = h(rho)g, depending on the depth, the liquid's density, and the acceleration due to gravity, but not on the shape of the container.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: What pressure is exerted at a depth of 2 m in water of density 1000 kg/m3? (g = 10 m/s2)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Pascal's Principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is
options: transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid
reduced as it spreads through the fluid
transmitted only in the direction of the applied force
questions.explanation: Pascal's Principle underlies hydraulic machines: pressure applied anywhere to a confined, incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the walls of its container.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body of volume 0.002 m^3 is fully submerged in water of density 1000 kg/m3 (g = 10 m/s2). What upthrust acts on it, according to Archimedes' Principle?
questions.explanation: Archimedes' Principle: upthrust = weight of fluid displaced = (rho)Vg = 1000 x 0.002 x 10 = 20 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface that makes it behave like a
options: gas with no cohesive forces between molecules
rigid solid sheet that cannot be deformed
stretched elastic membrane, tending to minimise its surface area
questions.explanation: Surface tension arises from cohesive forces between liquid molecules at the surface, causing the surface to act like a stretched elastic skin that resists an increase in area.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The rise of a liquid in a narrow capillary tube is
options: directly proportional to the radius of the tube
inversely proportional to the radius of the tube
independent of the radius of the tube
independent of the surface tension of the liquid
questions.explanation: From h = 2T cos(theta)/(r(rho)g), the capillary rise h is inversely proportional to the tube's radius r, so narrower tubes produce a greater rise.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A liquid of surface tension 0.07 N/m rises in a capillary tube of radius 0.0005 m. Given (rho) = 1000 kg/m3, g = 10 m/s2, and the liquid wets the tube completely (cos theta = 1), what is the height of rise?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Liquid drops tend to form a spherical shape mainly because
options: spherical shapes have the greatest surface area for a given volume
surface tension acts to minimise the surface area for a given volume, and a sphere has the least surface area for its volume
gravity pulls all liquids into spherical shapes
questions.explanation: Since surface tension tends to shrink the surface to the smallest possible area, and a sphere encloses a given volume with the least surface area of any shape, small drops become spherical.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: According to Newton's law of viscous flow, the viscous force between adjacent layers of a fluid depends on the
options: velocity gradient between the layers, the area of contact, and the fluid's coefficient of viscosity
questions.explanation: Newton's law of viscous flow gives the viscous (drag) force as proportional to the coefficient of viscosity, the contact area, and the velocity gradient (rate of change of velocity) between adjacent fluid layers.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Terminal velocity is the constant maximum velocity attained by a body falling through a fluid when
options: the body's mass increases to infinity
the body stops accelerating due to running out of gravitational pull
the net force on it becomes zero, as the upward drag and upthrust balance its weight
questions.explanation: As speed increases, viscous drag increases until, together with the upthrust, it exactly balances the body's weight; from that point the body falls at a constant (terminal) velocity with zero acceleration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Stokes' Law gives the viscous drag force on a small sphere moving through a fluid as being proportional to the
options: square of the radius of the sphere only
coefficient of viscosity of the fluid, the radius of the sphere, and its velocity
cross-sectional area of the sphere only, independent of velocity
questions.explanation: Stokes' Law states F = 6(pi)(eta)rv, where (eta) is the fluid's coefficient of viscosity, r is the sphere's radius, and v is its velocity through the fluid.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A small steel ball falling through a viscous liquid eventually moves at a constant velocity. This occurs because
options: the ball's weight has increased to match the drag force
the liquid's viscosity has dropped to zero
the increasing viscous drag has grown to balance the ball's weight minus the upthrust on it
the ball has stopped experiencing gravity
questions.explanation: As the ball speeds up, viscous drag (which increases with speed) grows until, combined with the upthrust, it equals the ball's weight, giving zero net force and hence constant (terminal) velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A thermometric property is a physical property that
options: only changes at the boiling point of a substance
varies continuously and uniformly with temperature, and can be measured
questions.explanation: Thermometers rely on thermometric properties, such as the length of a mercury column or the resistance of a wire, which change measurably and consistently with temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The lower and upper fixed points used in calibrating a mercury-in-glass thermometer are respectively the
options: boiling point of mercury and freezing point of water
ice point (0 degC) and steam point (100 degC)
absolute zero and the steam point
questions.explanation: The ice point (melting point of pure ice at standard pressure, 0 degC) and steam point (boiling point of water at standard pressure, 100 degC) are the standard fixed points on the Celsius scale.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: What is 25 degrees Celsius expressed in Kelvin?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: What is 350 K expressed in degrees Celsius?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: What is 40 degrees Celsius expressed in degrees Fahrenheit, using F = (9/5)C + 32?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A clinical thermometer is designed with a narrow range (around 35 to 42 degC) and a constriction near the bulb mainly to
options: allow accurate measurement of body temperature and prevent the mercury from receding before it is read
questions.explanation: The narrow range gives fine precision around body temperature, while the constriction stops the mercury thread from flowing back into the bulb immediately after removal, allowing the reading to be taken afterward.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The linear expansivity of a solid is defined as the
options: increase in volume per unit original volume per degree rise in temperature
total increase in length regardless of original length
increase in length per unit original length per degree rise in temperature
increase in area per unit original area per degree rise in temperature
questions.explanation: Linear expansivity (alpha) = increase in length / (original length x temperature rise), describing how much a material's length changes per degree per unit length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A metal rod of length 2 m has a linear expansivity of 12 x 10^-6 /K. What is its increase in length when heated through 50 K?
questions.explanation: Expansion = L x alpha x (temperature rise) = 2 x (12 x 10^-6) x 50 = 1200 x 10^-6 = 1.2 x 10^-3 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For a given material, the area (superficial) expansivity is approximately
questions.explanation: Since area involves two dimensions, the area expansivity (beta) is approximately 2(alpha), where alpha is the linear expansivity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For a given material, the volume (cubic) expansivity is approximately
questions.explanation: Since volume involves three dimensions, the cubic (volume) expansivity (gamma) is approximately 3(alpha), where alpha is the linear expansivity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The anomalous expansion of water refers to the fact that water
options: contracts when heated from 0 degC to 4 degC, and expands above 4 degC, with maximum density at 4 degC
contracts continuously as it is heated from 0 degC upwards
has the same density at all temperatures
expands continuously as it is heated from 0 degC upwards
questions.explanation: Unlike most substances, water shows unusual (anomalous) behaviour: as it is warmed from 0 degC, it first contracts until 4 degC (its point of maximum density), then expands normally above 4 degC.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The anomalous expansion of water is significant in nature because it
options: causes ice to float and allows ponds to freeze from the top, letting aquatic life survive underneath
prevents any ice from ever forming on water surfaces
causes all water bodies to freeze completely solid in cold weather
makes water boil at a lower temperature at high altitude
questions.explanation: Because water at 4 degC is denser than ice or colder water, ice forms and floats at the surface, insulating the water below and allowing aquatic organisms to survive through winter.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The ideal (general) gas equation relating pressure, volume, and temperature of a fixed mass of gas is
questions.explanation: The ideal gas equation PV = nRT combines Boyle's, Charles's, and the Pressure Law, relating pressure (P), volume (V), number of moles (n), the molar gas constant (R), and absolute temperature (T).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has a pressure of 100 kPa and volume of 2 m^3. If the volume is reduced to 0.5 m^3, what is the new pressure (Boyle's Law)?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A fixed mass of gas at constant pressure occupies 2 litres at 300 K. What volume will it occupy at 600 K (Charles's Law)?
questions.explanation: By Charles's Law, V1/T1 = V2/T2: V2 = V1T2/T1 = (2 x 600)/300 = 1200/300 = 4 litres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A fixed mass of gas has pressure 100 kPa, volume 3 litres and temperature 250 K. It is changed to pressure 150 kPa and temperature 300 K. What is its new volume?
questions.explanation: Using the general gas equation P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2: V2 = (P1V1T2)/(T1P2) = (100 x 3 x 300)/(250 x 150) = 90000/37500 = 2.4 litres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the pressure exerted by a gas on the walls of its container is due to
options: chemical reactions between gas molecules and the container
the weight of the gas molecules pressing down on the walls
the continuous collisions of rapidly and randomly moving gas molecules with the walls
the gas molecules being permanently attached to the walls
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory explains gas pressure as the cumulative effect of a huge number of molecules in random motion continually colliding with and rebounding off the container's walls.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: According to the kinetic theory of gases, at absolute zero (0 K, or -273 degC), the gas molecules would have
options: the same kinetic energy as at room temperature
questions.explanation: Absolute zero is the theoretical temperature at which the random translational kinetic energy of gas molecules would fall to a minimum (ideally zero), which is why 0 K represents the lowest possible temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The heat capacity of a body is defined as the quantity of heat needed to raise the temperature of
options: the body to its melting point
a unit volume of the body by ten degrees
a unit mass of the body by one degree
the whole body by one degree (Celsius or Kelvin)
questions.explanation: Heat capacity (C) applies to a specific object as a whole, unlike specific heat capacity, which is defined per unit mass of a substance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Specific heat capacity of a substance is defined as the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of
options: a unit volume of the substance by one degree
the whole substance by any amount
a unit mass of the substance by one degree (Celsius or Kelvin)
one mole of the substance to its boiling point
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity (c) is defined by Q = mc(delta)theta, representing the heat needed per unit mass per degree temperature change.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 0.5 kg of water by 20 degC? (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kgK)
questions.explanation: Q = mc(delta)theta = 0.5 x 4200 x 20 = 42000 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The method of mixtures used in calorimetry is based on the principle that, assuming no heat is lost to the surroundings,
options: heat lost always exceeds heat gained
the final temperature always equals the average of the initial temperatures regardless of mass
heat gained always exceeds heat lost
heat lost by the hotter body equals heat gained by the colder body
questions.explanation: In an ideal (insulated) mixing process, energy conservation demands that all the heat given out by the hotter substance as it cools is absorbed by the colder substance as it warms, until they reach a common final temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: 200 g of water at 80 degC is mixed with 300 g of water at 20 degC. Assuming no heat loss, what is the final temperature of the mixture?
questions.explanation: Heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water: 0.2(80 - Tf) = 0.3(Tf - 20). This gives 16 - 0.2Tf = 0.3Tf - 6, so 22 = 0.5Tf, and Tf = 44 degC.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The latent heat of fusion of a substance is the quantity of heat required to change it from
options: one temperature to another without changing state
solid to liquid at constant temperature
liquid to gas at constant temperature
questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion is absorbed during melting (solid to liquid) at the melting point, without any accompanying change in temperature, since the energy overcomes intermolecular bonds rather than raising kinetic energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: How much heat is needed to melt 0.1 kg of ice at 0 degC, given the specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 336000 J/kg?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The latent heat of vaporisation of a substance differs from its latent heat of fusion in that it is the heat required to change the substance from
options: one solid phase to another solid phase
solid to liquid at constant temperature, rather than liquid to gas
liquid to gas (vapour) at constant temperature, rather than solid to liquid
questions.explanation: Latent heat of vaporisation is absorbed as a liquid changes to vapour at its boiling point at constant temperature, while latent heat of fusion applies to the solid-to-liquid change at the melting point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Conduction is the mode of heat transfer in which heat travels through a material mainly by
options: direct molecular/particle vibration and collision, without bulk movement of the material
the bulk movement of heated particles from one place to another
questions.explanation: In conduction, heat energy passes from particle to particle through vibration and collision (and, in metals, free electron movement), without any overall movement of the material itself, and is most effective in solids.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Convection is the mode of heat transfer that occurs mainly in liquids and gases, through
options: the conduction of heat along a solid rod
the actual bulk movement of the heated fluid particles
questions.explanation: Convection relies on heated fluid becoming less dense, rising, and being replaced by cooler, denser fluid, setting up convection currents that carry thermal energy through the bulk movement of the fluid.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A sea breeze, which blows from the sea towards the land during the day, occurs because
options: land heats up faster than the sea, so warm air over land rises and cooler air from the sea flows in to replace it
the sea heats up faster than the land during the day
the wind always blows towards the sea during the day
there is no temperature difference between land and sea during the day
questions.explanation: Land has a lower specific heat capacity than water, so it warms faster in sunlight; the warmed air above it rises, and cooler air from over the sea moves in to take its place, creating a sea breeze.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A land breeze, which blows from the land towards the sea at night, occurs because
options: the land remains warmer than the sea throughout the night
the sea cools faster than the land at night
land cools faster than the sea at night, so air over the sea remains warmer and rises, drawing cooler air from the land
convection currents cease completely at night
questions.explanation: At night the land loses heat faster than the sea (again due to its lower specific heat capacity), so the relatively warmer air over the sea rises and cooler air flows from the land to replace it, creating a land breeze.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Radiation, as a mode of heat transfer, differs from conduction and convection in that it
options: always requires the bulk movement of a fluid
can travel through a vacuum without requiring any material medium
requires direct contact between particles of a medium
questions.explanation: Radiation transfers heat via electromagnetic waves, which can travel through empty space, unlike conduction and convection, which both require a material medium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: According to Prevost's theory of heat exchange, a black body is one that
options: is a perfect absorber and a perfect emitter of thermal radiation, and all bodies continuously emit and absorb radiation depending on temperature
only absorbs radiation but never emits it
only emits radiation when it is heated above its own temperature by an external source
reflects all incident thermal radiation and absorbs none
questions.explanation: Prevost's theory states that all bodies constantly emit and absorb thermal radiation regardless of their surroundings' temperature; a black body is the idealised perfect absorber and emitter, with net heat exchange depending on the temperature difference between bodies.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate
options: only at the source of the wave
perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave
in circles around a fixed point
parallel to the direction of propagation of the wave
questions.explanation: A transverse wave (e.g. a water wave or light wave) has particles oscillating at right angles to the direction the wave energy travels, producing crests and troughs.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium vibrate
options: parallel to the direction of propagation, producing compressions and rarefactions
perpendicular to the direction of propagation
only when the wave is reflected
questions.explanation: Longitudinal waves, such as sound, have particles oscillating back and forth along the same line as the wave travels, creating regions of compression and rarefaction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The amplitude of a wave is defined as its
options: number of complete oscillations per second
time taken for one complete oscillation
maximum displacement from the equilibrium (rest) position
questions.explanation: Amplitude measures how far a particle moves from its rest position at the peak of its oscillation, and it determines the energy (and, for sound, the loudness) of the wave.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The period of a wave is defined as the
options: distance travelled by the wave in one second
maximum displacement of a particle from rest
time taken to complete one full oscillation (cycle)
questions.explanation: Period (T) is the time for one complete cycle of the wave; it is the reciprocal of frequency, T = 1/f.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The frequency of a wave is defined as the
options: time taken for one complete oscillation
number of complete oscillations (cycles) produced per second
questions.explanation: Frequency (f), measured in hertz (Hz), counts how many complete wave cycles pass a point per second; it is related to period by f = 1/T.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wave of frequency 250 Hz has a wavelength of 1.4 m. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Using v = f x wavelength: v = 250 x 1.4 = 350 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s and has a frequency of 170 Hz. What is its wavelength?
questions.explanation: Wavelength = v/f = 340/170 = 2 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A progressive (travelling) wave differs from a stationary (standing) wave mainly in that a progressive wave
options: transfers energy from one point to another as it travels through the medium
has fixed nodes and antinodes that do not move
questions.explanation: A progressive wave carries energy away from its source, with every particle eventually repeating the same motion at a time delay; a stationary wave, formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions, has fixed points (nodes) of zero displacement and does not transfer net energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a stationary wave, the distance between two adjacent nodes is
questions.explanation: Stationary waves have nodes (points of no displacement) spaced at intervals of half a wavelength, with antinodes (points of maximum displacement) midway between them.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wave completes one oscillation every 0.02 s. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency f = 1/T = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Reflection of a wave occurs when the wave
options: bounces back into the original medium after striking a surface or boundary
combines with another wave to change amplitude
bends around an obstacle in its path
changes direction while passing into a new medium
questions.explanation: Reflection describes a wave being turned back at a boundary, remaining in the same medium, with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Refraction of a wave occurs when the wave
options: is absorbed completely by the new medium
spreads out after passing through a narrow gap
combines with a similar wave to produce a stronger wave
changes speed and direction as it passes from one medium into another
questions.explanation: Refraction is the bending of a wave due to a change in its speed as it crosses a boundary between media of different densities (or optical properties).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Diffraction of a wave is the
options: spreading of a wave as it passes through a narrow gap or around an obstacle
bouncing back of a wave from a surface
combination of two waves to produce a new wave pattern
bending of a wave as it changes medium
questions.explanation: Diffraction becomes most noticeable when the size of the gap or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength of the wave, causing it to spread into the region behind the obstacle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Interference of waves occurs when
options: two coherent waves overlap (superpose) to produce a resultant wave of different amplitude
a wave reflects off a rigid surface
a wave is completely absorbed by a barrier
a wave changes speed on entering a new medium
questions.explanation: Interference results from the superposition principle: when two coherent waves overlap, their displacements add algebraically, producing points of reinforcement or cancellation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Constructive interference occurs at points where the path difference between two coherent waves is
options: a whole number of wavelengths (0, wavelength, 2 x wavelength, ...)
always zero regardless of the waves
an odd number of half wavelengths
exactly a quarter of a wavelength
questions.explanation: When the path difference equals a whole number of wavelengths, the waves arrive in phase and reinforce each other, producing maximum amplitude (constructive interference).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Destructive interference occurs at points where the path difference between two coherent waves is
options: an odd number of half wavelengths
questions.explanation: When the path difference is an odd multiple of half a wavelength, the two waves arrive out of phase and cancel each other, producing minimum (or zero) amplitude.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Polarization is a phenomenon that can occur only in
options: transverse waves, since longitudinal waves have no perpendicular vibration to restrict
both transverse and longitudinal waves equally
questions.explanation: Polarization restricts the vibration of a transverse wave to a single plane; because longitudinal waves like sound vibrate only along the direction of travel, they cannot be polarized.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Young's double-slit experiment, which produces a pattern of bright and dark fringes, is important because it demonstrates
options: the particle nature of light only
that light travels faster in denser media
the wave nature of light through interference
questions.explanation: The alternating bright (constructive) and dark (destructive) fringes observed can only be explained if light behaves as a wave capable of interference.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A diffraction grating produces a spectrum of colours from white light mainly by
options: refracting light through a single thick lens
reflecting light off a single polished mirror
diffracting and interfering light from many closely spaced slits, which reinforces different wavelengths at different angles
questions.explanation: A diffraction grating has many equally spaced slits; light diffracted from each slit interferes constructively at angles that depend on wavelength, separating white light into a spectrum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The mirror formula relating object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) is
questions.explanation: The mirror formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v relates the focal length of a spherical mirror to the object and image distances measured from the pole of the mirror.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The linear magnification produced by a mirror is given by
options: m = v/u = image height / object height
questions.explanation: Magnification compares how much larger or smaller the image is than the object, and can be found either from the ratio of image to object distance or image to object height.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For a concave mirror, the focal length is related to the radius of curvature R by
questions.explanation: The focal point of a spherical mirror lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature, so f = R/2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror, forming a real image 60 cm from the mirror. What is the focal length of the mirror?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A convex mirror always produces an image that is
options: real and inverted when the object is far away
magnified when the object is close to the mirror
the same size as the object at all distances
virtual, upright, and diminished, regardless of the object's position
questions.explanation: Because a convex mirror diverges reflected rays, it always forms a virtual, upright, smaller image, which is why it is used in vehicle side mirrors for a wider field of view.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A real image, as opposed to a virtual image, is one that
options: cannot be projected onto a screen
is always the same size as the object
is formed by the actual convergence of light rays and can be captured on a screen
questions.explanation: Real images result from light rays actually meeting at a point, so they can be focused onto a screen, unlike virtual images which are formed by the apparent divergence of rays.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A concave mirror produces a real image magnified 3 times when an object is placed 20 cm in front of it. What is the focal length of the mirror?
questions.explanation: Magnification m = v/u = 3, so v = 3 x 20 = 60 cm. Then 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/20 + 1/60 = 3/60 + 1/60 = 4/60 = 1/15, giving f = 15 cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When an object is placed exactly at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror, the image formed is
options: real, inverted, and the same size as the object, also at the centre of curvature
questions.explanation: At the centre of curvature (u = R = 2f), a concave mirror forms a real, inverted image of the same size, coinciding with the object's position at the centre of curvature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When an object is placed between the pole and the focal point of a concave mirror, the image formed is
options: real and the same size as the object
virtual, upright, and magnified, appearing behind the mirror
questions.explanation: For u < f, the reflected rays diverge and appear to come from behind the mirror, producing a virtual, upright, and magnified image, as used in shaving/make-up mirrors.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Snell's Law of refraction states that
options: refraction only occurs when light is reflected
n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2), for light passing between two media
the angle of incidence always equals the angle of refraction
questions.explanation: Snell's Law relates the refractive indices of two media to the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction, and follows from the change in wave speed at the boundary.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The refractive index of a medium can be defined as the ratio of the
options: angle of incidence to the angle of reflection
speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the medium
real depth to the refractive index
speed of light in the medium to the speed of light in a vacuum
questions.explanation: Refractive index n = c/v, where c is the speed of light in a vacuum and v is its (reduced) speed in the medium; denser media have higher refractive indices.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ray of light strikes a glass surface (refractive index 1.5) at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.explanation: By Snell's Law, sin(r) = sin(i)/n = sin(30)/1.5 = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333, so r = sin^-1(0.333) is about 19.5 degrees.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A material has a refractive index of 1.5. What is its critical angle for light travelling from the material into air?
questions.explanation: The critical angle C satisfies sin(C) = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C = sin^-1(0.667), which is about 41.8 degrees.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Total internal reflection can occur only when light travels
options: from a less dense medium into a denser medium
at an angle smaller than the critical angle
from a denser (optically) medium into a less dense medium, at an angle greater than the critical angle
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection requires light travelling towards a less optically dense medium and striking the boundary at an angle of incidence exceeding the critical angle, so that no light is transmitted and all is reflected.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a triangular prism, minimum deviation of a light ray occurs when
options: the prism is made of a material with refractive index 1
the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of emergence
the ray is totally internally reflected inside the prism
the angle of incidence is 90 degrees
questions.explanation: The condition for minimum deviation in a prism is that the light ray traverses the prism symmetrically, making the angle of incidence equal to the angle of emergence.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The refractive index of a liquid can be found using the formula
options: n = real depth x apparent depth
questions.explanation: Because refraction makes an object submerged in a denser medium appear closer to the surface (its apparent depth) than it really is, the refractive index equals real depth divided by apparent depth.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A swimming pool appears to be 2.25 m deep when its actual (real) depth is 3 m. What is the refractive index of the water?
questions.explanation: Refractive index n = real depth/apparent depth = 3/2.25 = 1.33.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Optical fibres transmit light signals over long distances mainly by relying on the principle of
options: total internal reflection at the boundary between the fibre's core and cladding
simple reflection off an external mirror
questions.explanation: Optical fibres are designed so light striking the core-cladding boundary always exceeds the critical angle, undergoing repeated total internal reflection and travelling long distances with little loss.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The thin lens formula relating object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) is
questions.explanation: For a thin lens, the same numerical relationship as the mirror formula applies: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, using appropriate sign conventions for real objects and images.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The power of a lens is defined as
options: always equal to 1 for a converging lens
the product of its focal length and its magnification
the square of its focal length
the reciprocal of its focal length in metres, measured in dioptres
questions.explanation: Lens power P = 1/f (with f in metres) is measured in dioptres (D); a converging lens has positive power, and a diverging lens has negative power.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A converging lens has a focal length of 0.5 m. What is its power?
questions.explanation: Power P = 1/f = 1/0.5 = 2 dioptres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image formed?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a camera, the lens forms an image on the film or sensor that is
options: real, upright, and the same size as the object
questions.explanation: A camera lens converges light from a distant object to form a real, inverted, and usually smaller image on the light-sensitive film or sensor.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Myopia (short-sightedness) occurs because the eye lens focuses images
options: in front of the retina, and is corrected with a diverging (concave) lens
exactly on the retina at all times
in front of the retina, and is corrected with a converging (convex) lens
behind the retina, and is corrected with a diverging lens
questions.explanation: In myopia, the eyeball is too long or the lens too powerful, focusing distant images in front of the retina; a diverging lens spreads the rays out before they enter the eye so the image falls on the retina.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) occurs because the eye lens focuses images
options: in front of the retina, and is corrected with a converging lens
behind the retina, and is corrected with a converging (convex) lens
behind the retina, and is corrected with a diverging lens
exactly on the retina at all times
questions.explanation: In hypermetropia, the eyeball is too short or the lens too weak, so near images form behind the retina; a converging lens adds extra convergence so the image falls correctly on the retina.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Presbyopia is an eye defect that occurs mainly due to
options: a permanent opacity of the cornea
age-related loss of the eye lens's ability to accommodate (change shape)
questions.explanation: Presbyopia develops with age as the lens becomes less elastic and the ciliary muscles weaken, reducing the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects; it is often corrected with bifocal lenses.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A compound microscope achieves much greater magnification than a simple microscope because it
options: uses a single very powerful converging lens
uses two converging lenses (an objective and an eyepiece), each contributing to the overall magnification
uses a concave mirror in place of a lens
relies only on diffraction of light
questions.explanation: The objective lens forms a real, magnified image of the object, which the eyepiece lens then further magnifies as a simple magnifier, multiplying the two magnifications together.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Sound is produced by
options: any stationary object placed in air
the flow of electric current through a conductor
a vibrating object that sets up compressions and rarefactions in the surrounding medium
the reflection of light off a surface
questions.explanation: Sound originates from mechanical vibrations of a source, which disturb the surrounding medium and produce alternating regions of compression and rarefaction that travel outward as a longitudinal wave.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Sound generally travels fastest in
options: gases, because their particles move freely
liquids, because they are denser than gases
solids, because their particles are most closely packed, allowing rapid transmission of vibrations
a vacuum, since there is no resistance
questions.explanation: The speed of sound depends on how quickly vibrations pass between particles; the close packing and strong intermolecular forces in solids allow sound to travel fastest there, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases. Sound cannot travel at all through a vacuum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The pitch, loudness, and quality (timbre) of a musical note are determined respectively by its
questions.explanation: Pitch depends on frequency, loudness depends on amplitude, and quality (which lets us distinguish instruments playing the same note) depends on the mixture of overtones present in the waveform.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Overtones are
options: the fundamental frequency of a note alone
sounds that are too high-pitched to be heard by humans
higher-frequency components (harmonics) that accompany the fundamental frequency and give a sound its distinctive quality
echoes produced by reflection of sound
questions.explanation: Overtones are additional frequencies (multiples of the fundamental) produced along with the fundamental note; their relative strengths give different instruments their characteristic timbre even when playing the same pitch.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The fundamental frequency of a closed (one end closed) pipe of length L, with speed of sound v, is given by
questions.explanation: A closed pipe supports a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so the fundamental corresponds to a quarter wavelength fitting the pipe length, giving f = v/4L.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The fundamental frequency of an open (both ends open) pipe of length L, with speed of sound v, is given by
questions.explanation: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so the fundamental corresponds to half a wavelength fitting the pipe length, giving f = v/2L.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A closed pipe of length 0.5 m resonates with sound of speed 340 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?
questions.explanation: For a closed pipe, f = v/4L = 340/(4 x 0.5) = 340/2 = 170 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An open pipe of length 0.85 m resonates with sound of speed 340 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Beats are heard when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies overlap, producing a
options: complete cancellation of both sounds permanently
periodic rise and fall in loudness at a beat frequency equal to the difference of the two frequencies
single steady tone equal to the sum of the two frequencies
questions.explanation: Beats arise from alternating constructive and destructive interference between two nearly equal frequencies, producing a throbbing loudness variation at a rate equal to |f1 - f2|.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two tuning forks of frequency 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. What beat frequency is heard?
questions.explanation: Beat frequency = |f1 - f2| = |260 - 256| = 4 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Conductors differ from insulators in that conductors
options: allow free (delocalised) charges to move easily through them
only allow heat, not charge, to move through them
completely block the movement of all charges
questions.explanation: Conductors, such as metals, have free electrons that can move readily under an applied electric field, while insulators hold their electrons tightly, preventing charge flow.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A gold-leaf electroscope is mainly used to
options: detect the presence of electric charge and determine its sign
measure the resistance of a conductor
questions.explanation: The gold-leaf electroscope detects charge because the leaf and the stem repel each other when both carry the same charge, causing the leaf to diverge; its sign can be tested by seeing whether divergence increases or decreases with a known charge brought near.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Coulomb's Law for the force between two point charges is expressed as
questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance separating them.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two point charges of 2 x 10^-6 C each are placed 0.3 m apart (k = 9 x 10^9 Nm^2/C^2). What is the force between them?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Electric field intensity at a point is defined as the
options: charge stored per unit potential difference
work done per unit charge moved between two points
force per unit positive charge placed at that point
product of charge and distance from the source
questions.explanation: Electric field intensity, E = F/q, describes the force that would be experienced by a unit positive test charge placed at a given point in the field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Electric potential at a point is defined as the
options: force acting on a unit charge at that point
rate of flow of charge at that point
work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point
total charge stored at that point
questions.explanation: Electric potential, V = W/q, measures the work done per unit charge in moving a small positive test charge from infinity (zero potential) to the point in question.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The capacitance of a capacitor is defined by the formula
questions.explanation: Capacitance is the ratio of the charge stored on a capacitor's plates to the potential difference across them, C = Q/V, measured in farads.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A capacitor stores a charge of 6 x 10^-4 C when a potential difference of 3 V is applied across it. What is its capacitance?
questions.explanation: Capacitance C = Q/V = (6 x 10^-4)/3 = 2 x 10^-4 F.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For a parallel-plate capacitor, its capacitance increases when the
options: plates are moved further apart, regardless of area
plate area decreases or the separation increases
plate area increases or the separation between the plates decreases
dielectric between the plates is removed
questions.explanation: Capacitance C = (epsilon0 x epsilonR x A)/d, so it increases with larger plate area A or smaller plate separation d, or with a dielectric of higher permittivity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 4 microfarad capacitor is charged to a potential difference of 100 V. How much energy is stored in it?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When capacitors are connected in series, the total (equivalent) capacitance is found from
questions.explanation: Series capacitors combine like parallel resistors: the reciprocals of the individual capacitances add, giving a total capacitance smaller than any individual capacitor, while in parallel, capacitances simply add directly.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The e.m.f of a cell differs from its terminal potential difference because the e.m.f. is the
options: voltage measured only when no current flows in an external circuit is possible
same as the terminal voltage under all conditions
total energy per unit charge supplied by the source, including the drop across its internal resistance
current supplied by the cell per second
questions.explanation: The e.m.f. represents the total electrical energy supplied per unit charge by the source, part of which is used up driving current through the cell's own internal resistance, leaving a smaller terminal potential difference when current flows.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A cell of e.m.f. 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 ohms delivers a current of 2 A. What is the terminal potential difference?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A potential difference of 24 V is applied across a resistor of resistance 6 ohms. What current flows through it?
questions.explanation: By Ohm's Law, I = V/R = 24/6 = 4 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The resistivity of a material is given by the formula
questions.explanation: Resistivity relates a conductor's resistance to its geometry: rho = RA/L, where A is the cross-sectional area and L is the length, a property intrinsic to the material.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wire of length 1 m and cross-sectional area 1 x 10^-6 m^2 has a resistance of 2 ohms. What is the resistivity of the wire material?
questions.explanation: Resistivity = RA/L = (2 x 1x10^-6)/1 = 2 x 10^-6 ohm-metres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Three resistors of 2 ohms, 3 ohms, and 5 ohms are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.explanation: In series, resistances add directly: Rtotal = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 ohms.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 20 V supply is connected across three resistors of 2, 3, and 5 ohms in series. What current flows in the circuit?
questions.explanation: Total resistance = 2+3+5 = 10 ohms, so current I = V/Rtotal = 20/10 = 2 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Wheatstone bridge circuit is used to
options: store electric charge for later use
accurately measure an unknown resistance by achieving a null (zero) deflection balance condition
measure current directly without any calculation
questions.explanation: A Wheatstone bridge balances four resistances (two known, one variable, one unknown) so that no current flows through a galvanometer bridging them, from which the unknown resistance can be calculated precisely.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A potentiometer is used to measure the e.m.f. of a cell accurately because, at the balance point,
options: no current is drawn from the cell being measured
the cell's internal resistance becomes zero
maximum current flows through the cell
questions.explanation: At balance, the potentiometer's slide is positioned so no current flows through the galvanometer branch, meaning the cell being tested supplies no current, so its full e.m.f. (undiminished by internal resistance) is measured.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A device draws a current of 5 A from a 220 V mains supply. What electrical power does it consume?
questions.explanation: Electrical power P = IV = 5 x 220 = 1100 W.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A resistor of 10 ohms carries a current of 2 A. What power is dissipated in the resistor?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Ferromagnetic materials such as iron, cobalt, and nickel are
options: strongly attracted by a magnet and can themselves be magnetised
only attracted when heated above their melting point
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials have domains that can align with an external magnetic field, allowing them to be strongly attracted to magnets and to retain magnetism themselves.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The magnetic field lines around a bar magnet
options: are always parallel straight lines with no curvature
emerge from the south pole only
only exist inside the magnet itself
emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole, forming closed loops
questions.explanation: By convention, magnetic field lines are drawn leaving the north pole, curving round, and entering the south pole outside the magnet, continuing as closed loops through the magnet's interior.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor forms a pattern of
options: no field, since only coils produce magnetic fields
concentric circles centred on the wire, with direction given by the right-hand grip rule
straight lines parallel to the wire
closed loops similar to a bar magnet
questions.explanation: A current-carrying straight wire produces a magnetic field of concentric circular field lines around it; curling the right hand's fingers in the field direction with the thumb pointing along the current gives the right-hand grip rule.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid is
options: identical outside and inside the solenoid
strongest at the centre of each turn but zero along the axis
strong and fairly uniform, resembling the field of a bar magnet
questions.explanation: A solenoid's many turns produce a strong, nearly uniform magnetic field along its axis, similar in pattern to that of a bar magnet, which can be strengthened with a soft iron core.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The angle of declination of the Earth's magnetic field is the angle between
options: the horizontal and the resultant magnetic field direction
geographic (true) north and magnetic north at a given location
the equator and the magnetic poles
questions.explanation: Declination describes how far magnetic north (the direction a compass needle points) deviates from true geographic north at a particular location on Earth's surface.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The angle of dip (inclination) of the Earth's magnetic field is the angle between
options: two magnetic poles of a bar magnet
the resultant magnetic field direction and the horizontal plane at a location
questions.explanation: The angle of dip measures how much the Earth's magnetic field tilts below (or above) the horizontal; it is 0 degrees at the magnetic equator and 90 degrees at the magnetic poles.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A steel bar can be magnetised by which of the following methods?
options: Heating it far above its Curie temperature
Leaving it in a region with no magnetic field
Stroking with a magnet, placing it in a solenoid carrying direct current, or induction from another magnet
Dropping it repeatedly on a hard floor
questions.explanation: Magnetisation methods include single/double-touch stroking with a permanent magnet, the electrical method (placing the material in a solenoid carrying direct current), and induction by bringing it near a strong magnet.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A magnet can be demagnetised by
options: cooling it to a very low temperature
placing it inside a solenoid carrying a steady direct current
heating it above its Curie temperature, hammering it, or applying a gradually decreasing alternating current
stroking it repeatedly with another magnet in the same direction
questions.explanation: Demagnetisation disrupts the alignment of magnetic domains, which can be achieved by heating past the Curie point, mechanical shock (hammering), or subjecting it to a decreasing alternating magnetic field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is given by
options: F = BIL, regardless of the angle between the conductor and the field
F = BIL sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the conductor and the field
questions.explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor depends on the magnetic flux density B, current I, length L in the field, and the sine of the angle between the conductor and the field, being maximum when the conductor is perpendicular to the field.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A straight conductor of length 0.2 m carries a current of 4 A perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 0.5 T. What force acts on the conductor?
questions.explanation: Since the conductor is perpendicular to the field, sin(90) = 1, so F = BIL = 0.5 x 4 x 0.2 = 0.4 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A moving-coil galvanometer works by using the
options: heating effect of a current passing through a resistor
force experienced by a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field to produce a proportional deflection
capacitive charging effect of a coil
chemical effect of current in an electrolyte
questions.explanation: In a moving-coil galvanometer, current through a coil in a radial magnetic field produces a torque proportional to the current, causing a pointer deflection that can be calibrated to read current.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced e.m.f. in a circuit is
options: only produced when the flux is constant
inversely proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux
directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linking the circuit
independent of the rate of change of flux
questions.explanation: Faraday's Law states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an e.m.f. proportional to how quickly the flux is changing, forming the basis of generators and transformers.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Lenz's Law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it
options: flows only in direct current circuits
reinforces the change in magnetic flux that produced it
opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it
questions.explanation: Lenz's Law is a consequence of the conservation of energy: the induced current creates its own magnetic field that opposes the original change in flux, requiring work to be done against this opposition.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating current is related to its peak value by
options: rms value = peak value x square root of 2
rms value = peak value / square root of 2
questions.explanation: For a sinusoidal a.c. waveform, the r.m.s. value (equivalent d.c. value for the same power dissipation) equals the peak value divided by the square root of 2, approximately 0.707 times the peak.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An alternating supply has a peak voltage of about 311 V. What is its approximate r.m.s. voltage?
questions.explanation: rms voltage = peak voltage / sqrt(2) = 311/1.414, which is approximately 220 V, the standard mains r.m.s. voltage in many countries.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A transformer's primary and secondary voltages are related to the number of turns on each coil by
options: Vp/Vs = Ns/Np only for step-down transformers
Vp x Vs = Np x Ns
