questions.explanation: An ideal transformer's voltage ratio equals its turns ratio: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, allowing the secondary voltage to be stepped up or down relative to the primary.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A transformer has 100 turns on its primary coil and 500 turns on its secondary coil. If the primary voltage is 20 V, what is the secondary voltage?
questions.explanation: Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np) = 20 x (500/100) = 20 x 5 = 100 V, since this is a step-up transformer (more secondary turns than primary).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In an a.c. circuit, the opposition to current flow due to a combination of resistance and reactance is called
questions.explanation: Impedance combines the effects of ohmic resistance and reactance (from inductors and capacitors) into a single quantity that determines the total opposition to alternating current in a circuit.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment led to the model of the atom in which
options: most of the atom's mass and all its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny, dense central nucleus
the atom has no internal structure at all
the atom is a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it
electrons orbit in continuously variable paths around a diffuse nucleus
questions.explanation: The unexpected large-angle scattering of some alpha particles showed that atoms have a small, dense, positively charged nucleus, with the rest of the atom being mostly empty space, replacing the earlier 'plum pudding' model.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Bohr's model of the atom, electrons occupy
options: continuously variable orbits of any energy
orbits that continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
a single shared orbit around the nucleus
fixed, discrete energy levels (orbits), only gaining or losing energy when jumping between levels
questions.explanation: Bohr proposed that electrons can only exist in specific quantised energy levels, remaining stable in these orbits unless they absorb or emit a quantum of energy while transitioning between levels.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The energy of a photon of electromagnetic radiation is given by the equation
options: E = mc, where m is mass and c is the speed of light
E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency
questions.explanation: Planck's equation E = hf shows that the energy carried by a photon is directly proportional to the frequency of the radiation, with h as the constant of proportionality.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A photon has a frequency of 5 x 10^14 Hz (h = 6.63 x 10^-34 Js). What is its energy?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Einstein's photoelectric equation is expressed as
questions.explanation: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by stating that the energy of an incident photon is used partly to overcome the metal's work function (W0) and the remainder becomes the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a photoelectric experiment, a photon delivers 5 x 10^-19 J of energy to a metal of work function 2 x 10^-19 J. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron?
questions.explanation: Maximum kinetic energy = hf - W0 = 5x10^-19 - 2x10^-19 = 3 x 10^-19 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect is the
options: maximum frequency of light a metal can absorb
minimum frequency of incident light below which no electrons are emitted, regardless of intensity
frequency corresponding to the work function divided by intensity
frequency at which the metal begins to melt
questions.explanation: Below the threshold frequency, individual photons do not carry enough energy to overcome the metal's work function, so no photoelectrons are emitted no matter how intense the light is.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: X-rays are produced when
options: slow-moving electrons are gradually accelerated in a magnetic field
fast-moving electrons are suddenly decelerated on striking a metal target in an evacuated tube
visible light is passed through a diffraction grating
questions.explanation: In an X-ray tube, electrons accelerated through a high voltage strike a metal (often tungsten) target; their sudden deceleration converts much of their kinetic energy into high-frequency electromagnetic radiation (X-rays).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The de Broglie wavelength of a moving particle is given by
questions.explanation: De Broglie proposed that all moving particles have an associated wavelength given by lambda = h/p = h/(mv), linking a particle's momentum to a wave nature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An electron of mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg moves at 2 x 10^6 m/s (h = 6.63 x 10^-34 Js). What is its de Broglie wavelength?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An alpha particle is
options: a helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons) with a low penetrating power, stopped by a sheet of paper
an uncharged particle with no mass
a high-energy electromagnetic wave with the highest penetrating power
a high-speed electron with a moderate penetrating power
questions.explanation: Alpha particles carry a charge of +2 and are relatively large and slow, so they are easily absorbed, being stopped by just a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A beta particle is
options: an electromagnetic wave with the highest penetrating power
a helium nucleus with very low penetrating power
a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus, with moderate penetrating power stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium
questions.explanation: Beta particles are fast electrons (or positrons) ejected from an unstable nucleus during beta decay; they penetrate further than alpha particles but are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Gamma radiation consists of
options: high-energy, high-frequency electromagnetic waves with the greatest penetrating power among the three types of radioactive emission
fast electrons with moderate penetrating power
helium nuclei with the lowest penetrating power
questions.explanation: Unlike alpha and beta particles, gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation with no mass or charge, and they require thick lead or concrete to significantly reduce their intensity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Radioactive decay follows the law
options: N = N0 x lambda x t
N = N0 e^(-lambda t), where lambda is the decay constant
questions.explanation: The number of undecayed nuclei N remaining after time t follows an exponential decay law from an initial number N0, governed by the characteristic decay constant lambda of the isotope.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The half-life of a radioactive substance is related to its decay constant by
questions.explanation: Half-life is the time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay, related to the decay constant lambda by T(half) = ln(2)/lambda, approximately 0.693/lambda.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive isotope has a decay constant of 0.0866 per day. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation: Half-life = 0.693/lambda = 0.693/0.0866, which is approximately 8 days.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive sample undergoes 3 half-lives. What fraction of the original radioactive nuclei remains?
questions.explanation: After each half-life, the remaining fraction halves: after 1 half-life, 1/2 remains; after 2, 1/4 remains; after 3, 1/8 remains, following (1/2)^3 = 1/8.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Nuclear fission is a process in which
options: a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy and usually more neutrons
two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus
electrons are removed from an atom's outer shell
a nucleus emits only gamma radiation without changing its mass number
questions.explanation: In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) captures a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing a large amount of energy along with additional neutrons that can sustain a chain reaction, as used in nuclear reactors.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Nuclear fusion is a process in which
options: a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei
a nucleus captures an external electron
light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing enormous energy
radiation is absorbed without any nuclear change
questions.explanation: Fusion combines light nuclei, such as isotopes of hydrogen, under extreme temperature and pressure to form a heavier nucleus, releasing far more energy per unit mass than fission; this process powers the Sun and other stars.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The binding energy of a nucleus is defined as the
options: energy needed to ionise the outer electron shell only
energy released when an electron is captured by the nucleus
kinetic energy of the nucleus as it moves
energy required to completely separate a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons
questions.explanation: Binding energy represents the energy that holds the nucleons together; it equals the energy that would need to be supplied to break the nucleus apart into separate, unbound protons and neutrons.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The mass defect of a nucleus is the difference between
options: the mass of the nucleus and the mass of the whole atom
the number of protons and the number of neutrons
the atomic number and the mass number
the sum of the masses of its individual nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus
questions.explanation: The nucleus has slightly less mass than the sum of its separate constituent nucleons; this 'missing' mass, the mass defect, is converted to binding energy according to Einstein's equation E = mc^2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Thermionic emission refers to the
options: emission of electrons from a heated metal surface, as in a vacuum tube cathode
emission of light from a heated filament
absorption of electrons by a cooled metal surface
flow of current through a p-n junction in reverse bias
questions.explanation: When a metal (the cathode) is heated sufficiently, some of its free electrons gain enough energy to escape the surface entirely, a process exploited in vacuum tubes and cathode ray devices.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A diode's key characteristic is that it
options: only conducts when connected to an alternating supply
blocks current in both directions at all times
conducts current equally well in both directions
conducts current readily in one direction (forward bias) and blocks it in the other (reverse bias)
questions.explanation: A diode's asymmetric conduction, allowing current to flow easily when forward biased but blocking it (aside from a tiny leakage current) when reverse biased, is the basis of its use in rectification.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A p-type semiconductor is produced by doping a pure semiconductor with
options: a metal with very high conductivity
a pentavalent (donor) impurity, creating free electrons as majority carriers
a trivalent (acceptor) impurity, creating holes as the majority charge carriers
questions.explanation: Adding a trivalent element such as boron introduces 'holes' (missing electrons) into the semiconductor's crystal structure, which act as the majority positive charge carriers in p-type material.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An n-type semiconductor is produced by doping a pure semiconductor with
options: an inert gas to reduce conductivity
a pentavalent (donor) impurity, creating free electrons as the majority charge carriers
a trivalent (acceptor) impurity, creating holes as majority carriers
pure silicon only, with no impurity
questions.explanation: Adding a pentavalent element such as phosphorus contributes extra free electrons to the semiconductor's crystal structure, making free electrons the majority negative charge carriers in n-type material.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A p-n junction diode is formed by
options: coating a metal plate with an insulating oxide layer
heating a pure semiconductor to a very high temperature
joining two identical n-type semiconductors together
joining a p-type and an n-type semiconductor, creating a depletion region that permits current flow mainly in one direction
questions.explanation: At the p-n junction, a depletion region forms where charge carriers have diffused and recombined; this region allows current to flow easily when forward biased but strongly resists current flow when reverse biased.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Half-wave rectification uses a single diode to
options: allow current to flow during both halves of each a.c. input cycle
convert direct current into alternating current
allow current to flow during only one half of each a.c. input cycle, blocking the other half
amplify the input a.c. signal without changing its frequency
questions.explanation: In half-wave rectification, the diode conducts only when it is forward biased, which occurs during one half of the a.c. cycle, producing a pulsating output at the same frequency as the input with the other half removed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Full-wave rectification, using two diodes or a four-diode bridge arrangement, produces a pulsating direct current output whose
options: ripple frequency is twice that of the a.c. input, giving a smoother output than half-wave rectification
ripple frequency equals that of half-wave rectification
current flows only during alternate cycles, exactly as in half-wave rectification
output is a smooth, ripple-free direct current with no further filtering needed
questions.explanation: Because full-wave rectification makes use of both halves of the a.c. cycle (with polarity reversed appropriately during the negative half), the output pulses occur twice as often as in half-wave rectification, producing a smoother, more easily filtered direct current.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A bridge rectifier achieves full-wave rectification using
options: a single diode and a large capacitor only
two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer only, with no other arrangement possible
a transistor in place of all diodes
four diodes arranged so that current always flows in the same direction through the load, without needing a centre-tapped transformer
questions.explanation: The bridge rectifier arrangement uses four diodes so that, regardless of which half of the a.c. cycle is present, current is always directed the same way through the load, achieving full-wave rectification without requiring a centre-tapped transformer.
